2095.heavy: No weight-conditioned rule is stated. Position is invariant (final). The source does note that 'monosyllables must be heavy, either with a long vowel or a final consonant or both' (p.105) and that minor syllables are light (Cʌ, CʌN), so in practice the stressed final syllable is always the heavy one and the unstressed initial always light (the Light-Heavy iamb); weight and position covary and cannot be separated in this language.
2095.prule: Stress on the word-final (major) syllable. Words are monosyllables or maximally disyllabic: the word-initial minor syllable (Cʌ, CʌN, N̩) of sesquisyllables is 'always unstressed', and the first syllable of the very small set of true disyllables (/ko.raɲ/ 'lord', /ka.mɔk/ 'knee', /tʃa.lot/ 'fall over') is likewise unstressed; sesquisyllables are analysed as Light-Heavy disyllabic iambs [(rʌ.ˈbɨŋ)].
2095.srule: Not mentioned in Butler 2014, ch. 3 (secs. 3.2-3.6, pp. 100-139 read): Bunong words are heavy monosyllables or single disyllabic iambs (minor/initial syllable unstressed, final syllable stressed), so no word is long enough to carry a secondary stress.

2098.dq: Tindal stress is almost always penultimate, but occurs word-finally in some words with final heavy syllables. Emphasis seems to cause stress to become word-final. This is problematic for my data, because many of the forms have been elicited in isolation, and words in isolation are often emphasized.
2098.heavy: Exceptions only: 'final heavy syllables' -- 'heavy' is not defined; sec. 2.1 gives the syllable as (C)V(V)(C) with long vowels and diphthongs. All seven final-stressed examples end in a closed or diphthongal syllable (-yón, -ós, -án, -áy, -áʔ, -áp, -ów), but tánay 'termite' (same final shape as waláy 'house') keeps penultimate stress, so a heavy final licenses but does not determine final stress.
2098.prule: Penultimate stress, quantity-insensitive default ('almost always penultimate'; stress is written in the paper only when it is not penultimate).
2098.srule: Not mentioned in Robinson 2005 (sec. 2 Phonology incl. 2.3.7 'Stress', pp. 1-10 read; only one stress per word is marked and only primary placement is discussed); Robinson 2006 sec. 3 likewise silent.
2098.quote: 2.3.7 STRESS. Tindal stress is almost always penultimate, but occurs word-finally in some words with final heavy syllables. Emphasis seems to cause stress to become word-final. 2100.dq: in Central, stress is initial in words that have lost the first vowel, but remains on the second syllable when the first vowel is preserved (as in the case of /a/): *bahˈša ‘buckeye’ > ba:ˈša compared to Southeastern bxa.
2100.dloc: Sec. 3.6 'Stress', author's Dec. 2020 draft p. 9; published chapter pp. 1223-1246, page not verified.
2100.heavy: No weight condition; Buckley 2019 slide 29 (= 2014 slide 31), on second-syllable forms: '– no effect of vowel length'.
2100.prule: Stress is bound to the root: on the second syllable of the word when a syllabic (instrumental) prefix precedes a monosyllabic root or when the root itself is disyllabic or longer (slides: matúl 'old lady', maʔá 'food', bayí:tʃʼ 'learned to talk', qa:wátan 'eat (habitually)'); on the first syllable when the word begins with an unprefixed monosyllabic root (lówa:tʃʼa:tʃʼ '(we) don't talk', mítaqʼ 'they say') or when the historical pretonic vowel has been deleted (draft: p’še, šba; slides: < *mihʃé-, < *duwéni). Buckley's analysis: left-edge extrametricality with stress at the left edge of the domain, blocked by a monosyllabic unprefixed root; lexical exceptions (loans, certain roots). Draft summary for Central: 'stress is initial in words that have lost the first vowel, but remains on the second syllable when the first vowel is preserved'.
2100.quote: Primary stress can be reconstructed on the second syllable of most words (McLendon 1973: 34). It falls on the initial syllable where the root is just one syllable in length; essentially, the stress does not move off the root of the word. 2101.dq: Since, to a great extent, the structure of the language is monosyllabic, tone rather than stress composes the sentence rhythm. However, in certain words where there are more syllables than one, it is found that a certain stress occurs on the syllable containing a long vowel (Doke 1925: 136) -- the stress remark is about individual polysyllabic words, explicitly set against sentence rhythm.
2101.dloc: Doke 1925: p.130 'The Main Features'; p.136 'Length and Stress'; pp.149-151 'IV. Tone'. Vedder 1910: pp.13-15 'Die Töne' (disyllable accent rule on p.15).
2101.heavy: the syllable containing a long vowel (Doke 1925: 136); vowel length is phonemic ('most vowels occur either long or short, and this length is at times a determining factor between words otherwise alike')
2101.dflt: not stated (most words monosyllabic; tone carries rhythm)
2101.prule: Doke 1925: 136 (hedged, weight-conditioned): in words of more than one syllable 'a certain stress occurs on the syllable containing a long vowel' (example ǂˀá:xobo, initial long-vowel syllable stressed in a trisyllable); the stress is non-distinctive and left unmarked ('This stress, naturally, it is unnecessary to indicate'). No window, no default for polysyllables without a long vowel, nothing on secondary stress. The prosodic core is a five-tone system (high-, mid-, low-level, falling, rising) on every syllable, lexically distinctive: 'Musical tone on each syllable practically takes the place of stress as it is found in non-tone languages' (p.130); 'tone rather than stress composes the sentence rhythm' (p.136).

Tone' read): the only stress statement is a single non-distinctive stress on the long-vowel syllable of polysyllabic words; nothing on secondary or rhythmic stress ('tone rather than stress composes the sentence rhythm').

Doke p.130: Vedder's Gaub speakers 'spoke a distinct dialect, though one undoubtedly belonging to the same tribe'. Not Ju|'hoan…
2101.exq_: No exceptions are stated; the rule's scope is itself hedged: 'in certain words where there are more syllables than one, it is found that a certain stress occurs on the syllable containing a long vowel ... This stress, naturally, it is unnecessary to indicate.' (Doke 1925: 136)
2101.tone: Doke 1925: five tones (high-, mid-, low-level, falling, rising), relative pitch, lexically distinctive (ts'i: 'wet' vs ts'i: 'mouth'; xana 'to scrape' vs xána 'dagga'); tone 'practically takes the place of stress as it is found in non-tone languages'; stress 'not so important a subject', non-distinctive, left unmarked, only the length-linked observation for polysyllables. Vedder 1910: the same five 'musikalische Töne' on monosyllables plus 'dynamische Töne' (Stärketon) on diphthongal monosyllables and a lexically varying Stärkeakzent in disyllables, which he himself says is hard to separate from tone and, when even, 'easily perceived as high tone'.

However, in certain words where there are more syllables than one, it is found that a certain stress occurs on the syllable containing a long vowel; for instance, [click]ˀá:xobo. This stress, naturally, it is unnecessary to indicate.

2103.prule: Primary ('strong') stress falls on the major syllable, which is the only syllable of a monosyllable and the last syllable of every disyllabic and trisyllabic word; stress is predictable and therefore unwritten in the phonemic transcription. quantity-insensitive: the final syllable is stressed whatever its shape.
2103.srule: Secondary ('weak') stress [ˌ] on every minor syllable, i.e. a closed non-final syllable: disyllabic type 2 [W.S] ([ˌsam.ˈkʰɯn] 'woman', [ˌtam.ˈlaːŋ] 'monitor'), trisyllabic type 1 [W.U.S] ([ˌtok.ka.ˈhɔːk] 'to snore'), trisyllabic type 2 [U.W.S] ([ka.ˌtɕʰoːp.ˈloːh] 'cramp'); open presyllables (C + /a, u, æ/) are unstressed ([kʰa.ˈmoː] 'stone', [U.S]). Conditioned by syllable type (closed vs open), not by position or alternation.

2105.tone: Cerma is a tone language. Hürlimann & Pike: four contrastive tones (high, low, upglide, downglide); 'Each syllable has a contrast of tone, but on nonstressed syllables only high versus low tone occurs' (p. 57); the full four-way contrast is confined to stressed syllables (pp. 56, 59); 'Cerman has an extensive system of morphotonemics' (p. 58). The other held primary, Lauber (SIL ms. 1979-80, ed. 2006, 2,406 lines), analyses the same language with two tonemes (H, L) and word-level tone schemes and never mentions accent or stress (a full-text search 'accent|stress|proémin' = 0 hits), i.e. Pike's stress is one analyst's culminativity analysis, not a consensus.

2106.heavy: Not weight-based. The stress-attracting property is a lexical high tone on the second syllable of the left-edge two-syllable window; syllable weight plays no role in rule (2.19). The only weight remark is outside the stress section: 'The language displays some marginal evidence for weight-by-position where coda consonants are counted as one mora, but in general syllables do not need to be distinguished from moras.' (ch.2 intro, p.54).
2106.dflt: First syllable of the stem (root or prefix+root) when the second syllable of the window bears no high tone.
2106.prule: Stress domain = the first two syllables of the root or prefix-root combination (extended into root+suffix or root+enclitic when the root is monosyllabic). Within this left-edge two-syllable window, stress goes to the second syllable if that syllable bears a high tone (Assign-to-H-tone); otherwise to the first syllable (First-syllable-stress). Exactly one stress per stress domain (obligatory and culminative). Stress is predictable, not lexical (p.41, p.54); the lexical contrast is a privative H tone (H vs toneless), so surface stress position within the stem (hana 'leave' [ˈhá.nà] vs haná 'vomit' [hà.ˈná]) follows from the lexical tone of the second syllable.
2106.srule: None: 'Stress is obligatory (at least 1) and culminative (no more than 1) in the stress domain. There is one and only one stress in the two-syllable window of the stress domain.' No secondary or rhythmic stress is described anywhere in §2.3 'Tone and stress' (pp.84-102 read); high tones outside the stem-initial window are tone, not stress (panabí [ˈpà.nà.βí], p.99).

2106.tone: Lexically contrastive privative H tone: 'Chácobo syllables either bear a single high tone or else are toneless. High tone never spreads to adjacent syllables' (p.54). Tallman keeps stress and tone as distinct phonological categories: stress is obligatory and culminative in its two-syllable stem-initial domain, H tone is neither (more than one H per H-insertion domain, ex. 2.26). Correlates: stress = intensity + pitch; H tone = pitch + vowel duration (Rabi/Rámi spectrograms, 5-speaker production study, Table 2.15; Tallman & Elías-Ulloa 2020 JASA abstract agrees: word-initial prominence by intensity, final H by F0). A stressed toneless syllable surfaces with low or mid pitch. H-insertion rule (2.23): insert H on the first syllable of an H-insertion domain if it has no H, so stress and H usually coincide on the surface. Author's own framing (p.101): 'Based on the phonetics it is not clear whether Chácobo should be regarded as a system that distinguishes two types of stress, two types of tone, or a mixed tone stress system. In this dissertation I assume that Chácobo can be described as a mixed tone-stress system, but I emphasize that it is not motivated by the phonetics of this language.' Earlier literature described three tones (Prost 1960/1967, Iggesen; SAPhon lists 'Tone' only) or lexical stress with stress-driven tone…

2107.heavy: 'First VCC/VVC heavy syllable) from end is stressed, provided it is not more than 3 syllables from end' (p. 42). In Owens's string notation VCC = vowel + two consonants (non-final closed syllable, incl. before a geminate: támmamat, bahaayímna, or final CVCC: bitímm, zibádd) and VVC = long vowel + consonant (non-final CVV: náadata, náada; or final CVVC: tináad, marḍáan). Final CVC (kátab, ḍárab, kábiš) and open CV/CVV finals do not count as heavy; they fall to rules 25-26.
2107.dflt: Antepenult if the word is exactly three short syllables (ḍáraba, kábiša, fíhimat) or if the penult vowel is epenthetic with no heavy syllable (budúxulu, burdúgula); otherwise penult (ḍárab, kábiš) or the only syllable of a monosyllable (ráaṣ, fóog); in 4+ syllable words with the last three open, penult with secondary stress on the fourth from the end (ḍàrabáta).
2107.prule: Rightmost heavy syllable (Owens's 'VCC/VVC': a vowel followed by two consonants or a long vowel followed by a consonant, i.e. non-final CVC and CVV syllables and final CVVC/CVCC; final CVC and open syllables are light) is stressed if it is within the last three syllables; with no such heavy syllable in the window, antepenult when the word has exactly three short syllables (CV́CVCV(C)) or when the penult vowel is epenthetic, otherwise penult (monosyllables on their only syllable). Ordered before this: a closed set of morphemes stressed finally (-í 'my', comparative aCCáC, singulative -á, adjectival -íy(y) before f.sg -e) and loans that keep source stress/tone. Prefixes an-, al-, am- are outside the stress domain.
2107.srule: Secondary stress on the fourth syllable from the end (two syllables before the penult primary) in words of four or more syllables whose last three syllables are open: ḍàrabáta 'she hit him', gàabaláta 'she met him', fìhimáta 'she understood him', gàyyamáta 'she stood it up' (Owens marks it with a grave accent). No secondary stress is described for other word shapes.

2109.prule: Lexical privative pitch accent: every syllable of a word is H (accented) or L, and the H/L pattern distinguishes words (minimal pairs át 'hand' / at 'eight', gác 'grass' / gac 'tree', ágE / agÉ / agE). Stress exists but is non-distinctive, phonologically ignorable and untranscribed; it is predictable from the pitch pattern: in monosyllables it falls on the H syllable; in words of two or more syllables it falls on the first syllable of accentless (all-L) words and on the accent-bearing syllable of accented words (in HH / HHH words on the first syllable only), heard at the H-to-L transition.
2109.srule: No phonological secondary stress: all stress is non-phonemic and untranscribed (Huziwara 2019 sec. 3.1). Phonetically, by lexical pitch pattern (96): HLH words = first syllable stressed + third syllable 'slightly' (若干) stressed; LHH and LLH = first syllable slightly stressed + third syllable stressed; LLL (and LL) = first syllable may sound slightly stressed because its pitch is a little raised (n.45); HHH, HHL, HLL, HH, HL = stress on the first syllable only.

2109.tone: The author classifies the system explicitly as an accent (presence vs absence of H on a given syllable, 'which' not 'what kind'), not tone, following Hayata 1999 (n.10), and treats the accent as phonemic, marked with an acute. H is not culminative: HH, HHH, LH, HLH words all occur ((87)-(96), pp. 71-72), so typologically this is a privative H/zero syllable-prosody system (restricted tone in Hyman's sense) rather than Japanese-type culminative accent. Stress is present but non-contrastive ('ストレスは音韻論的には無視してよいので表記しない'): on an H syllable (the first syllable in HH, HL, HHH, HHL, HLL and HLH words, but the final syllable in LHH words, (96e)), tending to be heard at the H-to-L transition (n.45), or on the initial syllable of all-L words. Earlier fieldworkers quoted in n.44: Yagi 1964b: 59 'a pitch accent like Japanese, rising vs falling types'; Maniruzzaman 1984: 75-76 'a tone or a similar feature... contrastive... al / ál'.

tn.translation: Chakma has distinctive pitch. The bearer of the pitch feature is the syllable of the word, and the high vs low pitch of each syllable distinguishes meaning. That is, the tonal feature in Chakma is an accent, where what matters is the presence or absence of a particular pitch on the syllable in question ('which' of high or low), not a tone, where the kind of pitch ('what kind') matters [n.10]. In this paper this distinctive pitch is simply called accent. ... This paper regards the accent as phonemic and marks high pitch with / ´ /. Besides pitch there is also stress, but since I consider it non-distinctive I do not recognise it as phonemic. ...

2110.prule: Fixed penultimate: stress is non-distinctive and completely predictable, on the vowel of a monosyllable and on the penultimate syllable of every polysyllabic word, with no reference to syllable weight; suffixation keeps it penultimate (béθa 'house' -> beθóxin 'your house'). 2110.srule: Not mentioned in Sara 1974, ch. Phonology sec. 1.0a 'Prosody of the word', p. 22 (the book's entire treatment of stress: one accent per polysyllable on the penult, nothing on secondary or rhythmic stress; volume search for stress/accent finds only vowel-allophony remarks pp. 34-37).
2110.quote: The accent (stress) in Chaldean is cumulative and has no distinctive function. Its position is completely predictable. In monosyllabic words, it falls on the vocalic element irrespective of other features, and in polysyllabic words it regularly falls on the penultimate. It functions as the principal reliable phonological demarcative feature indicating word boundaries. /béθa/ 'house' /beθóxin/ 'your house'

2113.prule: No stress-placement rule is stated by any reachable source. Albornoz 1691 (the only grammar written while the language was spoken) says only that a long ('–') vs short ('^') 'acento' on a given vowel distinguishes many words (nolō 'snake' vs nolô 'flower, mat'; nacouī 'boy', narîma 'light') and singular vs plural (nahuī 'woman' vs nahuî 'women'); Adam 1887 adds 1st person = 'accent long', 3rd person = 'accent bref'. Montoya 1789 marks 'where the force of the pronunciation falls' word by word (two marks = both vowels long) and states no rule; in his 1789 list the mark sits on the final syllable in roughly two thirds of accent-marked forms (reader tallies 188/278 and 210-221/311), penult in ~65-74, antepenult in ~21-23. Whether Albornoz's 'acento largo/breve' is vowel length, tone or stress is undecidable from the colonial sources (Müller 1888 reads it as quantity of the final vowel).
2113.srule: Not mentioned in Albornoz 1691, Arte de la lengua chiapaneca (BnF Américain 38), Cap. 1 fol. 1r-1v and accent notas fols. 3r-3v, 7r, 11v, 13v: one largo/breve mark per word, no second prominence described. Montoya 1789 (apud Del Carpio-Penagos & Álvarez-Vázquez 2014: 215) on his doubly-marked words: 'sí en un termino se ponen dos, es porque ambas son largas' (both vowels long), i.e. not a secondary stress.

2113.tone: Albornoz's contrast is between a 'largo' (macron) and a 'breue' (circumflex) accent on one vowel of the word, distinguishing lexemes (nolō 'la culebra' / nolô 'la flor i el petate'; ndoma 'la garrapata' / ndoma pronounced 'breue' = 'el mais que va cresiendo', fol. 7r), singular from plural (nahuī / nahuî) and person. The mark sits on the final vowel in nolō, nolô, nahuī, nahuî, nacouī but on the penult in narîma 'la lus' (fol. 1v), and Cap. 2 nota 3a (fol. 3v) locates it by syllable for nouns/adjectives in -me: 'la primera i segunda persona se distinguen en los acentos largos en la ultima silaba, i la tersera breue; el cihmimo en la ultima largo, el cimemo en la penultima es tambien largo'. Müller 1888: 'verschiedene Quantität des schliessenden Vocals' (vowel quantity); Brinton 1886 calls it 'accent' and says his authorities' acute 'appears to be syllabic'; Montoya 1789 marks 'donde cae la fuerza de la pronunciación', two marks = 'ambas son largas'. None of the colonial sources uses the word tone; the held survey Campbell 2017 (Otomanguean historical linguistics, sec. 3) gives the modern view: 'All Otomanguean languages appear to be tonal... while the Chiapanec records remain ambiguous for tone or accent, any traces of these are always on final syllables (Fernández de Miranda & Weitlaner 1961: 18)'. The primary modern interpretations (Fernández de Miranda & Weitlaner 1961; Rensch 1976; Aguilar Penagos 2012) were not reachable.

tn.translation: [in the accents of the words] … with these two signs (–) (^) those that are long or short in the accent will be distinguished, attending to the syllable on which the said vowel stands … if it is long this sign (–) marks it and if short this one (^), e.g. nacouī 'the boy', narîma 'the light'. And this warning is not superfluous, for there are so many words that are distinguished only in the accents, e.g. nolō long 'the snake', nolô short 'the flower and the mat'. Likewise with the short or long accent the plural is distinguished from the singular, e.g. nahuī long 'the woman' sg., nahuî short 'the women' pl.

2115.prule: Lexical word tone, no stress rule: three contrastive tones (rising, falling, level); every independent word (any word other than a suffix, enclitic or grammatical auxiliary) carries exactly one contrastive tone regardless of its number of morphemes; the first tone of a phrase imposes its pitch shape on the whole phrase; tone glide falls on the first syllable of monosyllables and on the second syllable of longer sequences. 2115.tone: Ray 1966 sec. 13.4: 'a system of lexically significant pitch shapes, or tones' -- rising /^/, falling /v/, level (unmarked); one and only one contrastive tone per independent word; the first tone dominates the phrase; sec. 13.5 says only that 'Intonational stresses and lengths are strikingly different from those of the standard' (pre-pausal syllable-final lengthening, e.g. /^bhHalo/ terminated by [ʔ:], /nam/ by [m:], /nhag/ by [gk:]) and gives sentence-final contours, never a word-stress position. The falling-tone examples (hat 'hand', bhHalo 'good', dhan 'paddy', ThanDa 'cold', loDi 'stick') pattern with historical aspirates/h, as in the instrumentally established Sylheti tonogenesis. Ray warns (p. 89) that 'The description here is based on an inadequate sampling and an equally inadequate analysis, but may still provide some orientation.' The only positional accent statement in any source opened is older and hedged: Pargiter 1886 p. 68 item (6), copied by Grierson 1903 LSI V-1 p. 293: 'In words of several syllables, especially those borrowed from Persian and Arabic, the accent is thrown back as far as possible, and the following syllables are lightened' (i.e. retracted/initial accent with reduction of post-tonic syllables), illustrated only with two Perso-Arabic loans (haoyala 'charge' > haola; elaka 'connexion').

2119.prule: Stress falls on the final syllable of the phonological word, the 'main syllable'; the one or two optional presyllables that precede it carry lighter stress. The word template ((PS2)PS1)MS makes the stressed syllable obligatorily word-final, so stress is fixed, quantity-insensitive and computable from syllable count (1-3 syllables).
2119.srule: No category called secondary stress is named. No word exceeds three syllables, so no rhythmic stress arises.

2121.dq: Strong stress in words is generally on the vowel of the root, with secondary stress on final syllables.

2121.prule: Primary ('strong') word stress falls on the vowel of the root, i.e. it is anchored to a morphological unit (roots are mostly CVC monosyllables; with aspect/person prefixes and derivational/inflectional suffixes the stressed syllable's position in the word varies with morphological composition), hedged 'generally'; secondary stress on final syllables. Stress is not contrastive and not written in the ALMG orthography.
2121.srule: One secondary stress on the word-final syllable: 'Strong stress in words is generally on the vowel of the root, with secondary stress on final syllables'; Hopkins's stress-marked transcription shows final marks beside root marks (péká7, 7ókés, kálnél, kaníh). Non-iterative; no alternating rhythm described.

2121.cfw: Hopkins 2021, restating the phonology of his 1967 field study of San Mateo Ixtatán Chuj, puts strong stress on the vowel of the root with secondary stress on final syllables, and his stress-marked texts and 2012 dictionary transcriptions show the pattern (yík'ti'al, k'úhalil, kícham, stúkwi), while the only dissent, Domingo Pascual's 2007 normative grammar for the Academia de Lenguas Mayas, says most words are stressed on the final syllable but gives no rule and no marked examples and is plainly the weaker source; the other works read (Buenrostro 2013, Royer et al. 2020 and 2025, Bennett 2016, the 2007 pedagogical grammar) say nothing about placement.
